speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased and happy to be able to rise this afternoon to speak in favour of the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer). It is rather disturbing that I must rise again, on the twenty-first day of December, to speak with regard to a Bill which is not in the spirit of Christmas but, rather, one which takes away from a

December 21, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
segment of our populace something which they would have and could have if it were not for the application of this particular Bill. Someone has even used the terms "robbing" or "theft". The Bill, 1 suggest to Your Honour, is not in the spirit of Christmas, and the amendment which has been brought forward by my colleague is one which can only do the very least which can be expected for our senior citizens, a group of people which has been trampled upon by Bill C-131.
Put simply, the amendment asks the Government to put into words, into some form of substance, what it has been saying. If, as the Government Members claim, this Bill seeks only a two-year sacrifice on the part of our senior citizens, then let it cast that limitation in stone and not leave them in a position of doubt, or in any doubt whatsoever, as to the nature, time and extent of the sacrifice that it is asking this group whose working days are over to bear. No doubt they are being asked to bear a load which they should not be asked to bear when it comes to fighting inflation.
As is often the case, examples speak much louder than words or any other form of argument, and should this Bill pass without my colleague's amendment, senior citizens receiving the Old Age Security will be limited to a 6 per cent cost of living increase in the year 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984, regardless of what the inflation rate might be. In 1985 it has been said that full indexation will be restored. That is the issue which is before us this afternoon.
The Minister, in rather harsh words, has ridiculed the amendment brought forward by my colleague in our attempt to minimize the impact of this Bill on senior citizens. Today * she pointed out, with some personal pride, that inflation is below 10 per cent. For whatever reason the inflation rate has been reduced to a single-digit rate, it is still more than the rate of six and five.
In response to the comments of the Hon. Member who spoke previously this afternoon, I want to say that, of course, senior citizens are not so selfish that they are not concerned with the affairs and problems of other Canadians. They want to share the fight against inflation with all of us, but they want all of us to fight that battle of inflation equally, and they should not be in the forefront of the Government fight against inflation. The point, which I emphasize again, is that the inflation rate is not yet down to 6 per cent, to say that they will not suffer any loss is an absolute absurdity.
The level of assistance which the Government is fixing for senior citizens is below the present level of inflation and below the level anticipated by any Hon. Member in the House for the next two years, so that there will be a cost to our senior citizens. It has been emphasized again, so many times, that costs among our senior citizens vary. The application of a flat percentage rate on income leaves a disparity in purchasing power which, as was mentioned here this afternoon, amounts to the difference between the Minister and myself as a backbencher. That 6 per cent rate has a bearing on my purchasing power. However, our concern and that of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North, is with the great number of persons who are at or near the poverty line. It is this group
of people whom we want to protect by means of this amendment.
This amendment seeks to put those seniors, in the year 1985, in the same position as they would be if this Bill were not implemented. If the Bill is implemented, then they will be hurt for years after 1985 by reason of the application of the six and five formula which Government Members so proudly echo and present to the public across the country. This amendment calls on the Government to restore the Old Age Security recipient to the position he would be in as of January, 1985 if the Bill does not go into effect. What could be more fair than that? We have asked the senior citizens to bear the sacrifice for two years, but the Government should at least put them back in the position, as of January, 1985, that they would be in without the Bill. In other words, the amendment would write "Paid" on the senior citizens' invoice, and would let those senior citizens carry on without the drag of the continuing, battered, damaged luggage of the Trudeau years through the rest of their years by reason of the Government's action here at Christmas time in 1982.
Surely the amendment is in keeping with the Government's intentions, as has been expressed by all. It is a two-year program, it is said. However, I have not heard one statement from any Government Member to the effect that senior citizens would not and should not go on hurting after that two-year period; and if I am wrong, I would like to know which Government Member believes that Old Age Security should be permanently reduced. We on this side would not want to leave the impression that the amendment would be the end of our opposition to the Bill.
I had the opportunity of speaking in opposition to the Bill at second reading and, after reading the minutes of the committee meetings which have taken place from that time until today, I am even more strongly opposed today than I was then. At second reading I made the point that the money being taken from senior citizens could and should come from a wholesale war on Government waste, and that point still stands. We have yet to see any meaningful program of effort on the part of Government to cut the frivolous advertising, the parties, the JetStar extravangances or the public relations exercises.
While the Government asks senior citizens to take six and five, all MPs received a large binder of high quality reproductions of very dusty old news or press releases issued on the six and five program, which binder itself has no greater use than to gather dust on the shelves of so many. And at what cost? It was at the cost of thousands of dollars which, much more readily and to a greater national benefit, could have gone on to protecting our senior citizens. Rather than imposing the Bill which is being proposed today, the Government should cease wasteful spending.
Last June, when the six and five program was announced, we on this side were hopeful, anticipating that the Government was serious in its attempt to fight inflation and bolster the economy. We thought that that restraint would be the order of
December 21, 1982

the day, that it was only the forerunner of many such programs still to come. However, how badly we were mistaken! We should have known better. The six and five program is nothing more than a slogan to sell the Liberal Party, with selected, specific segments of our economy being asked to carry the brunt of the Government's attack on its program of restraint. Bill C-131 is a heinous example.
Senior citizens are not organized in this country, at least not as well as they might be. They do not have a union to lobby and fight on their behalf. They are not going to get any tax compensation, as will be the case for the Family Allowance recipient. In other words, the Government has picked on one of the most defenceless segments of our society, and that, Mr. Speaker, is offensive to us on this side of the House.
I would like to indicate why I feel this Bill should be withdrawn, and if the Government refuses to withdraw the Bill why my colleague's amendment should pass and why it is so important that it should pass. It was learned in committee that the June forecasts about this measure were wrong. This is not the first time this Government has goofed, has been found to be wrong. We all remember the 1980 forecast of cheap gas and low interest rates, not to mention the great disparity in the budget deficit proposals and forecasts. This is just one more of this Government's goofs. Last June, and I emphasize this, the budget forecast a saving to the treasury of some $105 million by limiting the Old Age Security increase to six and five. Now the Government claims that the saving will be only $84 million. That is $32 million next year and $52 million in 1984.
This amount may not be much in the Government's program of expenditure, and if it is not much, then why do they want to introduce the Bill at all? But I want to emphasize with all the force at my command that $84 million, when broken down, has a great impact on the standard of living of senior citizens. It would only take our Party one hour to eliminate the waste from departmental spending and make up that $84 million. Where is the sense, Mr. Speaker, of putting senior citizens through this kind of misery when far more could be saved by practising a modicum of in-House restraint?
In committee the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) argued that senior citizens would not be hurt and that the sacrifice which was being asked of them was small. We heard that said again today. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the jury is still out as to the amount of the sacrifice and how small the impact of this Bill will be on those persons. The point I want to make is there is fear, frustration and anger present among the senior citizens. These senior citizens continue to see their rents go up, food prices rise, gas and oil prices move upward, at the whim of a greedy Government and in response to its own scrambling to make ends meet. Our seniors among us see a Government imposing a six and five program on them for propaganda purposes. They see themselves not only as being abandoned, but abused for political purposes. As the saying goes, "It's not just the money".
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
What kind of Government is it that would want to leave the impression, as they do with this Bill, that senior citizens can fend for themselves in these difficult times? The Government and the Minister of National Health and Welfare can talk all they want, but what will be the perception which this Bill will leave across our country? Eighty-four million dollars is a paltry sum, yes, to the Government; but compare that to the toll it will take on our senior citizens.
There is another important aspect of this amendment. With an aging population, the federal Government has to be concerned with pensions. Two weeks ago we saw the introduction of the green paper on pension reform, which is an indication that some action is being taken to begin the difficult task of meeting the needs of people in crisis. And fundamental to any pension program is its protection against the ravages of inflation. At second reading, I quoted the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as being aghast at any thought that any pension program should not have an inflation program included, and this was part of his statement to the pension conference a very short number of years ago. In committee, witness after witness made the same point, expressing some concern at the message that this would give to the private sector. And after all that was said, here is the federal Government throwing indexation out of the window unilaterally, as in the case of Bill C-133, and giving the lie to every utterance which has been made on pension and pension reform and the necessity for protection against inflation. If it is all right for the Government to adjust pensions mid-stream, then why not the private sector? The Government's response to that is yes, these are extraordinary times and this Bill is of limited duration. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the private sector might be tempted to use that very same argument. There is every incentive here for them to do so. If the Government can do it, why cannot they?
Contrary to what Government Members are saying, the effect of this Bill is to reduce Old Age Security in perpetuity if they do not adopt the amendment put forward. No one knows for certain just how much they might be asked to bear. We do not know what the rates of inflation are going to be in the future, but we all know that senior citizens will be suffering the brunt of this restraint program today and in the next two years, and unless we adjust this Bill they will continue to suffer the disadvantage of these two years.
Therefore, there is only one way to guarantee that the sacrifice is for two years only. There is only one way to guarantee that neither the public nor the private sector will change the rules mid-stream, and that is to adopt the amendment put forward. The message to the private sector should be clear, and it is that this Bill is part of an over-all response to an economic crisis, that after the duration of that response these pensioners will be returned to the status they would have enjoyed in 1985 if it were not for the implementation of this Bill. With this amendment in place, there would be no long-term advantage to cutting pensions, and it would go a long way towards soothing the legitimate concerns of senior citizens. It would demonstrate a modicum of good faith at a time when there is very little faith in this Government's program of words and actions.

December 21, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, 1 would be remiss if I did not voice my objection to the concern and anxiety being shown by this Government to find an acceptable accommodation with Public Service pensioners, when no such concern is present for those citizens being hit by this particular Bill. I recognize that there are difficulties, there are technicalities, which permit such a distinction to be made; but surely the principle is the same. Public servants are paying into a superannuation account on the understanding that their pensions will be fully indexed, and taxpayers are remitting tax in the belief that Old Age Security would be fully indexed. In both instances it was the Government of Canada which indicated that such would be the case. I defy any Government Member to go out and tell any old age pensioner that there is a distinction they should be prepared to accept between themselves and a federal public servant now on pension. Why should they? How can we justify treating old age pensioners differently because one worked for the federal Government, and one did not? Yet here are two Bills which seek to break promises made, one Bill receiving the benefit of brinkmanship negotiations, and the other being raced through Parliament these few days before Christmas, and without any effort being made by the Government to act in good faith with respect to old age security recipients. We on this side believe that all pensioners have protection against the ravages of inflation, and therefore we argue that both C-131 and C-133 should be withdrawn.
The amendment, Mr. Speaker, is one of the bright aspects of this whole debate. The Bill is mean and underhanded, and if the Government is sincere about being honest with Old Age Security recipients, then it should adopt that amendment, and I am looking forward to the vote which might be taken on it.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in opposition to the Bill before us and to make some comments, although very brief, on the amendment, 1 would just like, first of all, to comment on the words of the last speaker, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), when he said it was unfortunate that these pensioners do not have a union to represent them. While that is true in the narrow legal sense of certification, representation and right to collective bargaining, pensioners across the country should know now, as they should have for years, that a number of unions in the country and the Canadian Labour Congress strongly support the cause of Canada's pensioners. Not only do they have unions defending their interests. Prior to 1926 and 1927, when the first minimal old age pension was introduced by two independent labour Members of Parliament, J. S. Woodsworth, and I believe it was Mr. Heaps, they were able to strike a bargain with the then Prime Minister, William Lyon Mackenzie King. They agreed to support the Government in return for the first old age pension legislation in Canada. So pensioners have had not only hundreds of individual unions and central labour bodies supporting them, but they have also had the full and continuous support of at least one political party. Pensioners have also had support from the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. I would like to read one very brief paragraph from that organization's submission as regards
this Bill and the Bill dealing with the partial deindexation of Family Allowances. It says:
In both these cases, family allowances and old age pensions, the scenario is the same. On one hand, reductions are made in the real value of benefits of a universal nature which have been advantageous mainly to women and, on the other hand, payments are made to those who belong to low-income families. The CACSW fears that through such measures, a gradual transformation of our income security system is sought in order to force adults to become increasingly dependent on each other within the family and to become eligible for benefits from government income security programs only if they prove they belong to a low-income family.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing wrong with attempting to strengthen the family, but there is something terribly wrong in forcing people into situations that they might not otherwise choose to be in. This Government, Mr. Speaker, in one way or another, is now attempting to force people off a secure and independent means of living and back into a situation which they would not individually and freely choose.
I mentioned that pensioners have the full support of the Canadian Labour Congress. 1 have before me a letter from Dennis McDermott, president of the CLC, which presents in great detail the arguments of that Congress and working people all over the country on behalf of our senior citizens. 1 would like to quote from it briefly. It reads:
At first blush, the effects of Bill C-131 are quite straightforward. Canadians over 65 whose incomes are high enough that they are not entitled to full or partial benefits under the Guaranteed Income Supplement program will simply be denied the full indexing of OAS benefits. Canadians over 65 whose incomes are low enough that they arc entitled to at least some GIS benefits will also have their OAS indexing capped. But for this latter group, supplemental GIS payments will be made that will make up for the capping of the indexing payments under OAS.
These apparently simple arrangements will have several particularly negative effects during 1983 and 1984, and these negative effects may be further accentuated after 1984. In brief these negative effects are:
(1)	the pension system as a whole will become even more of an income-tested
system;
(2)	the value of Old Age Security benefits will be reduced even further in
relation to pre-retirement earnings;
(3)	promises made to Canada's elderly will be broken.
I would like to dwell on the last sentence of that letter for just a moment, the matter of broken promises to Canada's elderly. In a brief presented to the committee dealing with Bill C-133, the Letter Carriers Union of Canada had something else to say about the trust in the Government. I think this is particularly important in light of the Government's apparent launching of an over-all review of Canada's entire pension system. If people do not have any faith in the ability of the Government to keep its word, what is the sense of all the talk, dollars, time and thousands of pages of printed matter? What is the sense of discussions concerning whether or not the pension system in the future will be believable or whether people can count on it for the security they require from any pension system?
The Letter Carriers' Union of Canada presented a brief to the Committee dealing with Bill C-133 in which it indicated:
December 21, 1982

According to past custom, it has been the invariable practice of former Presidents of the Treasury Board to consult the Advisory Committee on all matters affecting public service pensions. On this occasion, the President has not done so-
This comment referred to the time when the Public Service superannuation fund was launched, at which point the Government asked that it be excluded from collective bargaining and, in return, the Government of the day promised to make no unilateral changes to the pension plan. It broke that word. It regarded that commitment as a scrap of paper. It was torn up. Later in the brief the union continued:
If the government proceeds with the unilateral appropriation of funds from its former employees and those who are soon to retire, the terms "pension rights', "pension credits" and "entitlements" will cease to have any meaning whatsoever. The raid by the Treasury Board, Canada's largest employer, on the pension fund of its employees provides a truly frightening example for the private sector.
Also it provides a terrible example for the rest of the public sector and for people dependent upon the basic Old Age Security Program and the Canada Pension Plan. Over the past few years all of us have heard grave doubts voiced about the viability of the Canada Pension Plan and its ability to provide the pensions which the Government, Parliament and Canada as a country are committed to providing. If the Government demonstrates once more that its word cannot be believed, where will it leave us?
The Minister talked about the psychological impact of her programs. There is a psychological impact here-total destruction of faith on the part of any Canadian who wants to believe that when his or her representative in Parliament or in Government makes a commitment for the future, in fact it will be kept. They cannot believe that any longer. We have had many examples in Bills C-124, C-131, C-132 and C-133 of a Government which breaches contracts, commitments and its word. I cannot call such activity by its proper name here, but 1 believe people know what it is. It is not very pleasant.
Finally in its brief the union indicated:
If the Government succeeds in raiding the employee pension fund, how long will it be before it uses the same tactic again?
It concluded:
The Government proposal indicates that Canada is a very bad credit risk.
That is another reputation which we do not really need, particularly at this moment in our history.
1 referred to those comments even though some of them were outside the narrow scope of the legislation immediately before us in order to talk about the crisis, the problems and the psychological war, the one the Minister does not intend but which is being waged here.
I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared in The Vancouver Sun on December 17, 1982, entitled, "Question of integrity". It referred to upcoming revisions in the Canada Pension Plan and in part read:
It could be argued that the integrity of the Canada Pension Plan was endangered from the time of its inception in 1966-from the moment the federal government compromised the ideal of pay-as-you-go and made it possible for provinces to borrow an amount proportional to the contributions paid by their residents.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
But that wouldn't get us out of the crisis we're in today, with every province in debt-and indebted to the CPP for something like $22.4 billion in loans-or protect us from the crunch expected within two years when, without any payback by the provinces, employers and employees will be looking at higher contributions.
Once again the warning is clear. The Government has been in power for almost the entire period, except for that nine-month interlude, encompassing the building of the Canada Pension Plan and all the years since then. It has so mismanaged the affairs of the country that just one or two years down the road we may well face a time when we will have to tax people double in order for them to receive the benefits for which the Government has told them they have already paid.
Is what the Minister and the Government doing today just part of the so-called psychological war? Is it just a wish to find another sword in the arsenal for the six and five war against inflation, or is it a set-up for something broader? 1 am sure the Minister will say that we have to believe her. Many people believed her and the Government, and it is not doing them much good right now. The Government seems obsessed with this war against inflation and with talking about restraint. Conservative, New Democratic and Liberal Members have said that there is nothing wrong with restraint. We believe in restraint; we also believe in freedom. When the Government sets a goal around which society can unite and it invites people to participate, that is one thing; but when they are conscripted into an army to become involved in a Dieppe raid as part of its so-called war against inflation, that is another story. It is conscription; it is not asking people to join voluntarily in a united national cause. For them to pretend that some people do not like compulsion or Governments which break their words is pretty phony from that bunch over there.
I should like to refer to an article entitled, "They still worry about inflation?" which appeared in the December 7, 1982 edition of The Gazette of Montreal. Don McGillivray, the columnist, wrote the article from which I should like to quote four paragraphs because it carried a message about the war against inflation and how it perverted much of what has happened in the country. He wrote:
It will seem grotesque, a few years from now, that in the eighteenth month of the 1980s depression some people were still arguing that the main foe was inflation.
It will seem even more grotesque that these people were not a collection of economic flakes and nuts but ministers of finance and governors of central banks.
We know what has happened to the unemployment figures in the last few months. He continued:
A worldwide economic slump that has continued for a year and a half without an end in sight is the kind of crisis Canada faced in the 1930s.
Although Gerald Bouey, the governor of the Bank of Canada, talks about past years as the time of the Great Inflation, this crisis far outranks anything Canada has faced in the past decade.
Inflation was a puzzle that defied solution.
But it was not destroying jobs, homes, companies, industries and even countries the way this depression is.
I want to reinforce that paragraph and Mr. McGillivray's message. As long as people within society-pensioners, mothers, families, workers and small business people-were keeping

their relative positions to each other, not suffering unduly and seeing themselves fall lower on the totem poll of society, as long as the purchasing power of Canadians was keeping its relative position in terms of the economies of other countries- and that is what indexing was all about in terms of its impact upon people keeping their relative positions in society-then who really gave a damn? But the menace of depression is much more real. We don't have to go to other countries for examples. We've had depressions in Canada at least four times in our history.

Three million unemployed?
Two years of depression?

1 see my time is expiring, Mr. Speaker. I would end by saying that, while my colleagues and I have had a quick look at it, I am sure we will be supporting the Conservative amendment in this case and opposing, of course, Bill C-131. Mr. Speaker, as I was saying when the House took recess at 6 o'clock, it is basically dishonest for a political party to always advocate budgetary cutbacks and less Government spending and to oppose legislation which has a specific impact on a special group because this Party believes that, by so doing, it can score political points.

It is very important that the recipients of Old Age Security realize that all we are doing with this Bill is to indicate that indexation will be limited to 6 pe cent and 5 per cent in the next two years. There is no cutback on Old Age Security. There will be an increase of 6 per cent on January 1 and 5 per cent the year after.
Not only will those whom the legislation has described as being in need, which means those who receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement, receive the full indexation, they will also be compensated for the fact that the indexation will be reduced to 6 per cent. Therefore, it is very important that the recipients of Old Age Security realize this.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I indicated earlier that it was not totally honest for the Members of the Conservative Party to attack any specific measure that is designed to restrict public expenditures or restrict income to Canadians when it is specifically before the House. But then, all I have heard for years from the Progressive Conservative Party is that there should be less Government spending and less social spending. They say we should balance the budget and reduce expenditures in Canada but as soon as you bring a specific measure, they cry wolf. They say, my God, this is going to affect these people, those people and the other ones.
We cannot have a restrictive fiscal policy, if we want to be honest, that is not going to affect anyone. Of course it is going to affect people. What they are trying to do is to say we are for the principle of six and five per cent because that has an element of restriction of public expenditure and also of income. They say we are for that principle but when it is specifically going to affect anyone, we are against it.
I understand that position. If 1 were in the Opposition maybe I would see some advantage in doing that also. My purpose in speaking this evening is to assure those who receive Old Age Security that what they hear in these debates, that the Government is cutting back on Old age Security, is not true. They alluded, in the debate on Bill C-132 and the debate on Bill C-131, to the fact that there are so many people living at the poverty line, and the Government is going to take something away from people living at the poverty line, but in fact nothing at all will be taken away from people who live at the poverty line with any of the measures arising out of the six and five program. Absolutely nothing will be taken away from poor families by Bill C-132, or from retired people who rely only on old age pensions, if they receive the supplement. Nothing will be taken away from them and they will continue to be fully indexed. It is important that they see the difference between this and what the Official Opposition sees as a way to gain political points.
I do not speak of the NDP, because that Party's position has been well known. It is that Governments should never do anything about inflation, should never take anything away from anybody, should always give more. I do not object to that position, philisophically or intellectually, because sometimes 1 think Governments should do even more than what the NDP proposes, but it is important for the Canadian public and for those who are recipients of Old Age Security to see the politics in their position. The NDP has always been consistent in saying that we should spend more, we should do more, regardless of what the income to the Government is going to be, we should go into an unlimited deficit. Well, the Canadian public knows better and they know that the Government has to be responsible.
Even the members of the labour unions whose leaders support the NDP-obviously not all the members support the

We must check what the Government is doing, because it is the Government's responsibility to deal with these particular problems. In the first place, inflation is an increase in the quantity of money and credit. The money supply and the credit supply are increased in relation to the available goods and services. One definition is "too many dollars chasing too few goods". I am not sure that that is entirely applicable today. Certainly, there is an increase in the quantity of money and credit in relation to the available goods and services. In other words, there is too much money in the country. As a result, the prices soar. The market will bear more, so prices rise. I will not state it so simply that it sounds as though one pushes a button and solves the problem. I realize the seriousness of the problem, but I think that unless we get right down to the fundamentals and understand what we are trying to do, we are not likely to find a solution which will be workable.
One cause of inflation and, consequently, high unemployment, is unbalanced budgets. It does not happen overnight, but Governments which go on spending more than they have, not having the courage or desire to increase their revenue in order to have the money to spend, create a condition which helps to make the country ill. That is exactly one of the things which has been going on. Since the advent of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), we have almost ceased hearing about balanced budgets. However, each year the expenditures continue to rise, without the money to pay for them. Therefore, it is no wonder that we finally came to the place where the country could not stand that type of thing. The Government was aggravating the illness, making no attempt to try to clear it at all by raising the revenues which could have been raised in those better years.
If there is no increase in wages for our workers, and producers push up the prices, what happens? Producers simply sell less because the workers are unable to buy goods without increased wages. In that type of situation, there is a reduced output. When there are fewer goods and fewer people are buying, more workmen are put out of work as they are not required.
When we start to point our fingers at the cause, let us not point them at the workers of this country who have been trying to make both ends meet. In my view, it is completely unfair to say that the workers are the cause of inflation. They are affected as a result of inflation. They must have enough to eat, and either they receive increases in their wages, or else they go without many of the things that they would otherwise buy. If they go without, that means there are fewer and fewer demands and more and more people being put out of work. Nor can one blame the producers or the sellers. One cannot point one's finger at the producers, farmers and miners who create wealth in this country and say that they are the cause of inflation. They have been producing. One way of fighting inflation is to increase productivity.
There are two commonly known methods of dealing with inflation. One is to draw off the surplus money through taxes or through the method the Government is using with regard to

Well, Mr. Speaker, I have seen Mom since then. She said: "You know, son, I live in a senior citizen's apartment dwelling and I am enjoying my apartment and my way of life. "But", she said, "I can understand that I am not on the supplement and I, too, should be part of a battle which encompasses many sectors of society, both by law and the involuntary way by those people who cannot find jobs, and those people who voluntarily come along with the idea of the six and five program". So we say that this Bill is part of the over-all six and five program to help fight inflation and it requires the assistance of everyone to be effective. 1 believe the results of the last while show that in fact inflation is coming down. I regret very much that in debating on behalf of those people affected by such legislation, Members opposite, inadvertently, I think, are feeding the expectations of inflation forever. It will never, ever change by a point or two downwards because Members opposite keep telling us every day: no, it will never get down to 6 per cent so you, no matter who you are, if you are in business you had better ask for a 10 per cent increase for your product. If you offer a service, you had better ask for 15 per cent because inflation is never going to come down. So it goes, Mr. Speaker, that we hear the gospel of inflation as a fact of life from Members opposite.
I am sure that is not what they want. I am sure they know that we have to bring inflation down and that we have to be in a competitive position with the rest of the world. Current statistics indicate that we have not been doing very well but that now we are beginning to. I honestly believe, as I support the Bill, that we will see a time when the six per cent inflation rate will be the norm rather than the abnormal. But, for goodness sake, it cannot happen by itself. It has to happen with all of us urging people to get behind this country of ours and to bring their expectations into line so that the common good is served.
There are times when we forget what are our Party affiliations in the interests of the people of the country. Senior citizens have a great feeling for the country because they
helped build it. Also they have a great feeling for their children and their children's children. They would rather not have to accept less of an increase, but they will. They still say to me that they respect the fact that the Government is doing what it can and that they will join with many other sectors which have voluntarily and involuntarily joined the fight against inflation. They are willing to do their part, to accept their responsibility.
This piece of legislation, as unpalatable as it might be to some of us, is part of the great psychological battle we are fighting to demonstrate unequivocally to the people of Canada that we must have a lower inflation rate. It will be lower if we all accept it, but it will never go down if the leaders of the country keep going around telling people day in and day out that they are living in a dream world, that this will never happen, and that they have to prepare themselves for higher and higher inflation. This is the exact message which has been coming through this debate day in and day out, that inflation will not come down. They do not want it to go down; it is not in their political interests for the inflation rate to go down or for other things to happen in the country. I make a friendly, passionate plea to Hon. Members opposite and to the people of Canada that these are difficult times, but there is a glimmer of light ahead if we all work together to help bring down the inflation rate. If we work together we will enjoy even more this great country of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the Conservative amendment to Bill C-131. I must say that I have some concern about the amendment. Of course we do not want the Bill to be before the House. In fact, we think it should be withdrawn. There is no time like the present to do it just before Christmas. We understand that the amendment is really a grandfather clause which attempts to restore indexing at the same rate as it would have been in two years' time had there been no Bill C-131.
I am surprised that we have not heard Liberal Members supporting the amendment. It is one thing they could really support. This afternoon we heard the very jubilant Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) announce that inflation was now down to 9.7 per cent in Canada and that the Liberal program was working. Of course this is good news, especially just before Christmas. I am sure most elderly Canadians also felt the same way. These same Canadians, if they were aware of Bill C-131, unfortunately did not have enough time for their organizations to study the Bill. So often there is no adequate time for them to know, to react and to have input in Bills such as these, especially if they live in western Canada.
However, many of them know about this Bill which is designed to cut the indexing on their pensions in the new year.
I am sure they sighed a big sigh of relief this afternoon when they heard that inflation was going down. I am sure they thought that now the Government, thank goodness, does not have to use Bill C-131 to fight the war against inflation or to

use senior citizens and their pensions to fight the war. Certainly we can assume, even by Liberal logic, that if inflation is coming down there is absolutely no need for the Bill. I asked the Minister this afternoon that if that was the case, why did she feel the Bill was necessary. Of course those of us who were present heard her ridicule the question, as if 1 were insincere about it. 1 was certainly very sincere. I do not have the "blues", but she certainly passed it off as a ridiculous statement to think that she should withdraw the Bill penalizing senior citizens by cutting the indexing of their pensions. She continues to believe that the six and five will somehow win the war on inflation. I cannot grasp the logic of this Liberal policy.
It would have been good sense to withdraw the Bill because it costs a lot to prepare Bills and to go through the administrative procedures of processing and implementing them. I appeal to the Government-and I know the Conservative Party on my right shares our concern in this regard-to withdraw Bill C-131. Inflation is down. It will do nothing to reduce inflation further. Why should senior citizens be penalized in this way? However, I want to tell senior citizens that unfortunately the Government and the Minister in charge of the Bill are not logical. They do not act in a rational manner. They are not even humane at Christmastime. The Government intends to proceed with its very punitive Bill, and we oppose it very strongly.
I happened to hear on the radio today that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is doing his Scrooge act as well. He has declared that he will go ahead regardless of whether or not the Bill is passed. Let me now again refer to Bill C-131 and the amendment before us. I want to summarize again very quickly why the NDP opposes this Bill and will oppose it after we vote on the amendment.
We believe that old age pensions should not be subject to the six and five index cut in 1983 and 1984. I might also point out, as Liberal Members have not done, that there is absolutely no evidence we have been able to find that these cutbacks will be recovered after the two-year period. The Minister did not affirm that fact at the committee. That is why we have some interest in this amendment. We oppose the six and five restraint policy of this Government in general because it victimizes public servants, imposes an unfair cutback on the indexing of old age pensions, and also imposes the same kind of restriction on the Family Allowance payments to mothers and children.
The principle is the same in all these Bills. It is simply a Liberal policy of making the most vulnerable people pay. Under Bill C-124 the civil servants, who have no free right to speak out in protest, were the victims. Children have no voting powers, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not even process the recommendations of the committee to set up a secretariat for children which could at least speak out on their behalf. I am sure such a secretariat, had it existed, would have protested Bill C-132. We have spoken at other times about the unfairness of these Bills to women.
Bill C-131 is perhaps the worst Bill because it threatens to undermine the whole concept of universality of old age pensions. Again the Minister ridicules that suggestion, but I would remind her that practically every organization which had witnesses appear before the committee reaffirmed the position we have been espousing since the Bill first came before us, that is, that it does undermine old age pensions and the universal aspect of them. The Bill sends a signal to pensioners that their pension cheques will no longer be indexed to the real cost of living.
In British Columbia there are something like 285,000 old age pensioners, about 48 per cent of whom will qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement. They are the very poor with little or no other source of income. I expect the majority of the other 52 per cent who receive the old age pension and qualify only for that part of the program are also finding it pretty difficult to stretch their incomes. Indeed, many of them are

still living below the recognized poverty level. I have some facts which I will present in a moment that point out that they are finding it difficult to meet the high cost of living, those things they have to pay for out of their budgets. The cutback in the index will definitely take money out of the pockets of the pensioners, most of whom are on fixed and marginal incomes. They are not the very poorest of people, but they are certainly poor by most standards.
We observed some attempt today to get some facts on the cost of living in Vancouver, a part of which I represent. A very small, modest one-bedroom apartment there rents for a little lower than before, but still upward of $286 a month. Utilities cost $60 a month, and for people who have a home, property taxes are up. A telephone costs over $10 a month and food runs at about $180 a month. I think that is a very conservative estimate, if you will pardon that expression. Single pensioners, particularly, who do not have two cheques to cover these costs, with overheads of $540 a month minimum, are finding it very difficult. Most old age pensioners have very little left from their cheques, even if they do have supplementary pensions, so let us not kid ourselves that this cutback is hurting only the people who are not in need. That is a myth, and if the Liberals think that old age pensioners with these kinds of costs with low incomes are not in need, that shows their insensitivity.
The Minister also admitted that the savings from Bill C-131 and Bill C-132 would be relatively small in terms of cash to the federal Government. She has said that this is really not the major concern, but rather it is a means of fighting a psychological war. The Government is fighting this psychological war through old age pensioners in an attempt to bring down inflation. I still cannot figure out the rationale for that particular war. It seems to me what we need is a little psychoanalysis of the Government.
Fiscally the Bill will save only about $84 million over a two-year period. That is the best figure I have been able to get. That seems like a lot of money, particularly to an old age pensioner, but if we consider it in terms of federal budgets it is not a lot as we in this Elouse know. It is not a lot in terms of people in need. It is not a lot in terms of senior citizens who have contributed a lifetime to raising families, building communities, developing oui resource industries and, indeed, building Canada. It is certainly not a lot when compared to the expenditure which I quoted earlier in a former speech in terms of fighter planes, amounting to billions of dollars. Let us also consider the $500 million give-away to Dome Petroleum. If we want to find money in the kitty we should consider these areas.
The Liberal Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) said earlier that the Liberals are really helping senior citizens through the six and five program to cut back on the indexation of pensions. Can you imagine that, the suggestion that the Government is really helping senior citizens by cutting back on pension indexation?
The Hon. Member also said the Government is showing leadership. It is certainly typical of Liberal leadership: no price controls, no tax reforms to tax back the universal program, which is the best way to make it work, from those who earn over $100,000 and pay absolutely no income tax. Of course,
there is no economic strategy. The only leadership the Liberals are showing is in how to hit the public servants who do not have a voice to speak out on their own behalf, the children who do not have a voice on their behalf, the mothers at home raising those children and the senior citizens. I must say that is some kind of leadership.
The other day I spoke about how unfair this Bill is to elderly women who make up over 50 per cent of our old age pensioners. By far the greater proportion of those women are living below the poverty level. This is truly a tragic situation. Because they are poor they are isolated and lonely, not getting out very often, and thus are doubly discriminated against by age and sex. Most of them do not have the Canada Pension Plan or private pensions. They live longer than their husbands so they end up living as widows, single people, with the high costs coming out of one pension cheque. I have said many times in this House that we have heard this story over and over again from the women we visited during the work of the task force on older women. We heard the same story in every Province of Canada. Elderly women are in a desperate situation. Some of them receive the GIS and some are in the marginal group. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that they are very poor and do not have the money at the end of the month to put the necessary nourishing food on the table which they need. One woman spoke on a hot line show saying that she had to pay $200 for special medication. In that particular Province she had no means of getting this money back. Even if they have extra income, it is usually below the poverty line. It is much more difficult for single people to pay these costs from a single cheque.
I would also like to say that the Green Paper on pensions does not address this problem at all. There are no recommendations, much less solutions, in that Paper to deal with the poverty which elderly women are suffering from now. Women in two generations from now will not have an adequate pension plan.
As I asked previously, why are the Liberals placing this restraint program on the backs of elderly Canadians and Canadian families? Only a little money will be saved.
I can quote the Minister herself who said to the Canadian Congress on Pensions last spring. She said that senior citizens must have an adequate income and pensions which are fully indexed. She said:
Many women who previously had little more than a vague, often unreliable notion of what to expect from Canada's pension system have been jolted-
She went on to say:
It is therefore incumbent upon us to move quickly in meeting the challenges of pension reform.
She then said:
All pensioners should be protected from inflation; women must be treated more equally.
Of course, Bill C-131 denies those statements. Its effects will achieve the very opposite to what the Minister was advocating last spring.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to gather my thoughts and get back to the thrust of my speech. I was saying to senior citizens that, contrary to what certain Members would like them to believe, there is no question of cutbacks by the Canadian Government, the very Government which first came up with those various formulae such as the old age pension guaranteed income supplement. Quite the opposite. In 1983, the guaranteed income supplement will be fully indexed to the inflation rate. In addition, all senior citizens who receive the guaranteed income supplement will also get an extra amount which will compensate them for the difference between the 6 per cent increase in their basic pension and the actual increase in the cost of living recorded throughout the country. Now then, Mr. Speaker, why scare people who are asking for nothing more than security in order to be happy? Why should anyone make those people suffer by telling them that their monthly pensions might be reduced? Your pensions are going to be reduced! That Government is taking the bread out of your mouth! That is inhuman, Mr. Speaker.
It is quite proper for a politician to play politics, but not on the backs of poor people, not on the backs of those who are most in need of Government assistance, not on the backs of those who built our nation. The only thing the Government is asking from those who receive only the basic pension, who have other sources of income and who get at least $9,000 a year is to accept that their pension be indexed at 6 per cent this year instead of 7 per cent, 8 per cent or 9 per cent. It might very well be 6 per cent because, according to the news I heard this morning, for the first time in many months the rate of inflation for the past twelve months was 9.7 per cent, that is below the double digit bracket. And if we keep following our policy, I think that the rate of inflation will drop to 6 per cent or even less within a year. It goes to prove that we are being falsely accused of taking money away from the needy. The target of the Government, supported by Members of the Official Opposition who voted in favour of the six and five program, is to lower the rate of inflation which strikes hard at poor people. Mr. Speaker, does it make any difference to a millionaire whether the rate of inflation is 12 per cent rather than 6 per cent? Not really. Offhand, I would suggest that a millionaire does not know the price of a pound of butter. On the other hand, a senior citizen who has to live off his pension and the man who draws unemployment insurance benefits do know the price of a pound of butter, and they do know what 12 per cent means, Mr. Speaker. It is precisely to fight against misery that the Canadian Government has launched its six and five program. The Government will do its utmost to lower the rate of inflation which harms the poor and often is a boon to the rich. We want to bring it down to a level where poor people will at least be able to cope. Mr. Speaker, as a young Member

December 21, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
of Parliament, I cannot accept that people come here to scare our senior citizens who are already worried enough as it is. Look at them, Mr. Speaker, look at the NDP Members, at these minions of Mr. McDermott, come and see them in committee supposedly fight for a few dollars that the pensioners must give up if they want a lower inflation rate tomorrow. I asked them recently: Are you thinking about the 15,000 residents of the Lac-Saint-Jean constituency who are now unemployed? Are you thinking about the young people of 20 who are having problems?
Mr. Speaker, the only way that we can really protect the most needy is to break the inflation spiral and create jobs, more jobs and still more jobs, and this is what the Government is trying to do. One of the main problems of Canada in the last ten years was that there were not enough Liberal governments in the Provinces. For ten years, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government, which is a Liberal Government, has been fighting against flag-wavers in Quebec; it has been fighting against governments much more willing to increase their own powers at the expense of their own people than to defend them. That is the main problem. True liberalism, the liberalism which helped to build Canada during the past 100 years, cares more for man than for an ideology or for symbols. You know, Mr. Speaker, that to be a Liberal Member of Parliament does not mean that you belong to a union. It means that you are the representative of union members, pensioners, workers and unemployed. As for the New Democratic Party, it simply belongs to the unions. This is quite obvious in the various committees, Mr. Speaker. There is always a union advisor behind them. They call each other brothers and comrades. This is really something. We simply have to read last week's minutes of the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 am sorry to interrupt the Hon. Member, but I believe he is straying from the subject. I invite him to come back to it.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. 1 commend your great wisdom. Naturally, my great desire to help the senior citizens who will benefit from this six and five program causes me to stray from the subject under discussion. I admit it and I thank you for calling me to order.
What I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker, is quite simple, and that is that since liberalism is a philosophy which has brought about policies designed to help individual citizens, it is impossible for a Liberal Government to remove benefits, and I am thinking particularly about senior citizens when 1 say so. The facts are quite the opposite. What the Liberal Government has done this year, what it has done in the past and what it will do in the future is to help those who have built this country, those who have given us everything, and this is what we want to do as effectively as possible, not by giving them a few cents more this year, but by defeating inflation once and for all and
getting rid of an inhuman way of life which caused the most needy to be told: If butter is too expensive, do not eat any! Mr. Speaker, it is impossible to imagine that these people who have given so much to our country can today be the victims of prophets of gloom who would have them believe that their income will be cut this winter. That is not true. Why? Because when I myself, took on the duties of a Member of Parliament, when I was elected by my constituents, my only wish was to protect those constituents, especially the most needy, against any action detrimental to their interest and to their welfare. That is what I want to do and what I shall do as well as possible, and to do so, I cannot tolerate that anyone try to scare my constituents. I have already pointed out that, under the National Health and Welfare programs, and the Minister is here in the House, the Canadian Government will pay $21 billion this year to the provinces under cost-shared programs, and I want all senior citizens to realize that all these programs are indexed.
When an elderly person is treated, the Government of Canada pays at least 50 per cent of the bill. When an elderly person is attended by his or her physician, it is the same thing. When a senior citizen receives assistance from the Quebec Department of Social Affairs, for example, the Government of Canada pays at least 50 per cent of the bill. 1 want this fact to be known. And 1 want to say to all those individuals, it is not true, the Government of Canada means you no harm. If the Government of Canada has enough courage to say to its own officials, to those, and 1 hope you will allow me to say so, Mr. Speaker, who had to put up throughout the year with the strong pressures of a shaky economy-You know that the officials who work in our regional offices had to put up with the pressures brought to bear by the many unemployed who went to see them, people who needed a job or some assistance. Those people were asked to make sacrifices and they accepted. Why? They did so because they knew they could help their fellow citizens, the underprivileged, and contribute to reduce the inflation rate.
This is why they accepted, and if the government had the courage to ask them, it was not easy. I did not find it easy myself when I asked my own staff to agree to salary cutbacks and it was not easy either when I cut my own salary. Why was all that done? Because we no longer want our senior citizens to deal with the tremendous problem of inflation. We also realize that those people in need should not be given the bare minimum during a period of runaway inflation. Assistance should have a degree of stability. And I want to say to our senior citizens: Do not worry even though some would have you believe that there will be no spring nor summer next year. It is not true! The Government of Canada, that is the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) said during a televised interview, "This year we will launch a fight against poverty". If the Liberal Government has set up social programs to help
December 21, 1982

the needy, it will surely not remove them when more Canadians than ever need help. On the contrary, and this is what is going on now. That is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has been doing all along with his six and five program, and that is what we are doing now.
As to the Hon. Members who have voted in favour of the six and five program and who, for petty political reasons, are now voting against each and every clause or bill to amend the existing programs, I do not understand them. How is it possible to support a comprehensive policy and then vote against every specific bill? Only through cowardice, Mr. Speaker. Cowardice! It is always easy to hold back and say: I am in favour of this principle, but I cannot accept the fact that it may affect me. It reminds me somewhat of what is going on in the Province of Quebec. While they are imposing a 20 per cent cut on everybody, we are granting an 8 per cent increase. That is just about what the PQ members are saying nowadays. It reminds me also of the stand taken by the Progressive Conservative Party here. They say that they are in favour of the six and five program, that they are against inflation, but don't you dare change anything, you Government Members. That is not the way to build a country, Mr. Speaker, and especially not the way this country was built in the past. And there exist today a tremendous country called Canada, in case some people may have forgotten. Tremendous, indeed!
We are faced with problems today. As you know, because there is inflation, some people find it strange and wonder who is to blame. Ever since I came here, Mr. Speaker, a great many things have happened. I remember hearing Hon. Members of the Progressive Conservative Party say and even shout in the House that the Federal Government would not pay for Alberta oil, that it was not paying enough and should pay more for it. Is that not inflation, Mr. Speaker? Because of the problems we are faced with today, we must tell our senior citizens who are getting only the basic Old Age Security Pension, not those who are getting also the Guaranteed Income Supplement: You must accept an indexation capped at 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year of your Old Age Security Pension. Mr. Speaker, there is nothing that says that the inflation rate will not drop to 6 per cent in 1983. As a matter of fact, I am under the impression that the Government's policy is so successful that it might drop even lower. That is what is really great about it. I am dealing with the Canadian people openly and honestly, and I ask my colleagues here to stop frightening the disadvantaged. Let those who have built Canada enjoy a secure old age and retirement, where life will be as pleasant tomorrow as it is today and where they will be able to lead a peaceful and rewarding life.

speechtext: The time has expired. In fact, he has been allowed two minutes extra in compensation for interruptions. Is there unanimous consent of the House for the Hon. Member-there does not appear to be. The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin).

Mr. Speaker, there are several themes which are being promoted by different groups in the House as we listen to speeches on Bill C-131 which we have before us now, the effect of which really is to limit the increases which would have been experienced by people receiving Old Age Security to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in two successive years.
The theme we are receiving from the Government Members is that we are somehow trying to create an impression in the minds of people which will frighten them, or will concern them. Indeed, I think there are some basic issues which are of major concern, and those issues I would like to approach in just a moment. On the other hand, we are getting another kind of theme from the New Democratic Party, which is a little bit extraordinary. I see Members of the NDP standing up and criticizing this Party because we supported the six and five program. Indeed, that is true. The Conservative Party has supported in general the six and five program because who would not want inflation to be down at that level and interest rates down to that level? Who in their right minds would even suggest that that is not what would be good for the country at this time when we are experiencing the current economic distress? But I would like to make very clear to the NDP and the Government that what we have supported in the six and five program was the general thrust. We did not give a carte blanche to policies like this, or to policies which would affect the Family Allowances for children. Those types of specific policies, I believe, are a separate issue, and those are things we are very much opposed to, and are in fact debating now. But I Find it passing strange that the NDP would stand up on the one hand and talk about not supporting the six and five program, when the only specific thing that program did when it was first introduced, apart from any other legislation which we are getting now or that we will get, was to reduce the salaries of Members of Parliament. And the NDP voted en bloc against that.
I would like to approach this, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of some of the basic issues which we are being presented with by this type of legislation right now. This Bill proposes to reduce the amount, which has been committed by the Government and which was expected by people who are receiving Old Age Security across Canada over the next two years, by an amount that will be equivalent to approximately $300.
I think we have to take several things into consideration. First of all, the population is aging, some us faster than we would like. The fact is that in the last ten years there are over

December 21, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
700.000	fewer Canadians under the age of 20 and 800,000 more over the age of 60. Therefore, we are seeing a basic change in the population in Canada. This is an important factor in how we look at our programs and our social needs in Canada in the coming years. One of the major social problems which we face is the persistence of poverty. At this point in time at least 15.5 per cent of our population can be described, on the basis of certain income levels, as being below the poverty line.
We went through a period of time in the sixties and seventies when there were programs at the provincial and federal level which reversed that trend, where instead of increasing the number of Canadians who could be defined as living in poverty, we reduced that number. We went through a period of time then when there were many more families which had two people earning incomes, a wife starting to work or a husband starting to work, so there were two incomes coming into the family. There were the boom times of the seventies which all of us fondly remember where we reversed the trend of poverty. Now it is swinging the other way for a number of reasons. The economic policies which we have experienced over the last ten years, I would suggest, are one of the most important reasons for that. Apart from that, I think we need to be aware and accept the fact that we are dealing with people who are living in poverty in Canada and that number is going to increase unless we make some very basic changes.
In one of the counties which I represent they are looking at a welfare budget next year which will be 50 per cent higher than the welfare budget this year. In this year alone there are 500 more welfare cases than there were last year. Those changes are not something I am talking about in an abstract way. Those are things which are actually happening at the grassroots level of communities all across Canada. On the basis of national poverty levels, I believe there is an estimate that over
500.000	more Canadians during this next year or so will be facing the need for welfare assistance. That is a large number of people, Mr. Speaker, and it is an important factor in how we approach the eighties.
Another effect of this aging population is that we are looking at the need for significantly increased medical services. This is a question which I think is important and it can be addressed in several ways. It can be addressed by the federal Government trying to administer in a variety of ways the health care system in Canada. There is no question but that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has this kind of thing on her mind. It can also be addressed at the community level and at the individual level in a different fashion. But these are the needs and the circumstances which have arisen because of the aging population. There is one thing which the Minister said in a press release which I would like to read into the record. It reads:
The budget takes as a given that Canadians who are not in need are entirely prepared to share in serious sacrifices which are required to bring our country out of the economic crisis.
In a broad way, I do not doubt at all that Canadians en masse would support programs and efforts to take this country out of the kind of circumstances we have today, but I think the essential point is that we are dealing now in this Bill, and
particularly in this amendment, with a certain segment of Canadians to whom a commitment has been made by this Minister of National Health and Welfare and this Government, in fact by the Parliament of Canada. Now, for whatever reason, we have another proposal which is being championed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and which I find extraordinary, which will decrease that commitment. It is not a question of whether it is 3 per cent or 5 per cent, or what that percentage is, but the commitment had been made. People had made financial plans, understanding things to be a certain way as far as the commitment which the Government made is concerned, and now they are presented with a Bill which is going to change that commitment.
I would argue strongly on behalf of the group in our country which is in danger and which does have to make a disproportionate amount of sacrifice if we impose this kind of measure on them, that that commitment is clearly not going to be met by the Government. Now, we hear discussions about this being on the backs of those people. As I go through the areas I represent I think those are precisely the people who would be prepared to make sacrifices. I have to agree with the Government on that point. But I do not really think we can accept some of the Minister's arguments when she talks about the way she is first of all targeting in on those people who really need it. If she uses any kind of logic at all, she cannot deny the fact that what she is really doing is pushing more people into poverty, the people she made a commitment to.
We can get into a lot of political rhetoric at this time, Mr. Speaker. We hear it a lot, and strong political arguments are made by all sides. It is Christmastime and everyone likes to be generous at this time of the year, and we probably have but another 24 hours before most of us will be heading back to our constituencies. However, I think we are leaving while the Minister is reneging on a commitment made to Canadians who have contributed to this country and are now in a very vulnerable position. Now, $300 over two years is not much, but those people will be denied the security of knowing it will be there if needed.
I am not at this point, Mr. Speaker, arguing whether it is right or wrong to have universal programs, but I think it should be made very clear that the Minister has already given up the concept of universality. She can no longer argue that she supports universality. GIS is not a universal program. Health care benefits are not in a universal program. Whether they should be or not is a different argument, but I do not think she should go out and talk about these programs and the social welfare system in Canada as though it were a universal system. Clearly it is not.
The third thing I think we need to do is to consider the priorities of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and her Government. This measure might save $100 million. That is a significant amount of money, but we must balance that off
December 21, 1982

against other initiatives the Liberal Government has taken. As an example, the amount of advocacy advertising by the Government to promote the six and five program, which is in part a political response to a very serious economic situation, will eat up a considerable amount of the saving. What have we got to show for it at the end? Another high profile reflection of the Liberal Party. I think that is a serious concern, Mr. Speaker, because it extends not just into the six and five program but into the manpower programs, energy programs; indeed it is all around us. It has made the federal Government the largest single advertiser in the country. And all of us have to question seriously the priorities of a Government which decides that it will renege on a commitment for the sake of putting forward advertising slogans in an effort to explain itself, when in many cases the explanations lack even a reasonable degree of accuracy. Those points have been made by many others, but I think it is a serious question which should be answered.
I am going to close my remarks by asking the Minister a question. I wonder if she really believes that she is making any significant contribution to the economic recovery of the country, a contribution to the things which need to be done to create the kind of economic climate we want in Canada? Is she really fulfilling her responsibility to older people by proposing legislation like this? I suspect she will not answer that question directly. 1 suspect she will continue to suggest that this is a good thing on behalf of Canada. Elowever, I think there is a serious question concerning the kind of Cabinet measures she is supporting now and which it appears she will support in the futures. I think she has in fact, given up her constituency and that her constituency is very poorly represented in Canada today.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few brief comments on Bill C-131 before I call it ten o'clock. It is an important Bill, and simply because it does not affect a lot of people does not mean it is not important to the people it affects. There are some measures in the six and five program worthy of support in the sense that through them we try to impress upon people that inflation in many ways is psychological; that if the expectations are that inflation will come down in the future, in fact you may be able to do something about it. Inflation is what this Bill is all about, and the story is told that if we could give everyone a pill before they went to bed this evening to make them think there was going to be a depression in the morning, they would wake up and create the worst depression imaginable. Conversely, if you could convince people that tomorrow inflation was going to be at an end and economic good times were going to return, that expectation and belief would bring about the kind of economic recovery we all long for.
However, it is unfortunate that this six and five program is extended to cover people who, in large part, are unable to defend themselves against the worst effects of inflation. I refer specifically to the pensioners, Mr. Speaker.
Adjournment Debate
Now, I have seen figures which indicate that the Government anticipates saving anywhere from $40 million to $80 million by applying the six and five to the Old Age Security Act. But if you take that $40 million figure and equate it to total Government expenditure, we would save $1 out of every $2,000 the Government spends. Bill C-131, Mr. Speaker, would save approximately $1 for every $2,000 the Government spends. That is really not a lot of money when you consider the kind of people we are going to extract that $1 from. That to me is a sad commentary on how the Government chooses to fight inflation. It is even more lamentable when you consider the fact that in large part the people who are going to be adversely affected by this Bill are the ones who are in most need of the money.
I see you rising, Mr. Speaker; may I call it ten o'clock?
