METRIC CONVERSION-COMPULSORY ASPECT OF LAW ON ADVERTISING. (B) REQUEST THAT MEASUREMENTS BE PERMITTED IN BOTH IMPERIAL AND METRIC SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of being branded a dinosaur, as I was the other day in the House by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Berger), I want to deal with the Liberal Government's unholy zeal to force-march Canadians into metric conversion. My point in rising one more time on this subject is not only to express my disappointment and frustration at answers which I have received from the Government in recent months concerning the compulsory aspect of going metric, but to represent those Canadians who are genuinely concerned about their own democratic rights. These people number in the millions and they deeply resent the callous trampling of those rights by the federal Government.
Specifically, I have tried to obtain answers from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) to questions which I placed to him on April 2, 1982, on July 30, 1982, and just last week on December 15, 1982. All three questions were designed to get some honest response from the Government on a fundamental misleading of the public about the compulsory, mandatory nature of going metric, and metric only. It is my view that misstatements by the Minister and his Metric Commission to the people, to the press and to Parliament about the manner of metric conversion must be exposed for the misrepresentations they are.

December 21, 1982
Adjournment Debate
Let me cite three examples of flip-flops by the Liberal Government and a breaking of his word by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs with respect to metric conversion.
Example No. 1-the White Paper on metric conversion, tabled in the House of Commons by the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, now the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin), indicated that the metric process shall be voluntary. Page 5 of the White Paper specifically indicated:
No legislative action is contemplated which would make mandatory the replacing of inches and pounds with metric measure.
That was the basis on which the Government of the day received unanimous consent in the House. Members of Parliament of that day were clearly under the impression that metric conversion would be voluntary, and nobody objected to that democratic process. Well, how voluntary is it? Ask hundreds of thousands of small businesses and retailers across the country and, Mr. Speaker, you will learn how the Government disregarded and belied the spirit of its own White Paper.
Incidentally, it may interest the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who, I notice, is in his place with his carefully prepared answers to the points I am raising, that the same White Paper agreed that it was of major importance that Canada keep pace with the United States in converting to metric. The Liberals have changed their minds on that too, if we are to listen to the Hon. Member when he said, as reported on page 21774 of yesterday's Hansard'.
-just because the United States is doing something does not mean it is right . . . he is saying that just because the Americans are doing it, it is right.
Of course the Parliamentary Secretary was referring to the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm).
This brings me to example No. 2 of what I regard as false and misleading advertising. The Metric Commission persists in peddling the big lie that Canada must go metric because the United States is going metric. Exactly the opposite is true. The Americans have wound down their Metric Commission because of too much consumer resistance to changing to the new system, and Great Britain has slammed the brakes on metric conversion for the same reason. We are not going metric to join our major trading partners; we are going metric because the Government and the Metric Commission are telling us to go metric.
Speaking of the Metric Commission, I have been alarmed for some time about this huge bureaucracy which has become a law unto itself. It has spent hundreds of millions, indeed well over a billion, of Canadian taxpayers' dollars to force us into a system we have not asked for, do not need and cannot afford. The Commission spends hundreds of thousands of dollars on snazzy, flashy propaganda. As one Member of Parliament, I want to see a fully independent investigation of the activities of the Metric Commission over the last decade, at least. If the Auditor General's people are too busy to look into it, then the Government should appoint a judicial inquiry into the Metric Commission's service or disservice to Canadians.
Let me come, finally, to example No. 3 of the Government's flip-flopping and breaking its word to Canadians about metric
conversion. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has consistently left the impression with retailers, manufacturers, Canadians generally and the House of Commons specially, that the Government would not prosecute those who choose to retain imperial measurement if that is what consumers desire. The Government got its fingers burned over the Kasparian case in Calgary when Section 7 of the Weights and Measures Act was found to be faulty and prosecutions seemed to be out of the question.
We now have the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs saying, "That's it, boys-we're giving you one last chance. It's metric only from now on".
This is the Government which refuses to prosecute spies, but now says it will prosecute service station operators, including Members of Parliament, who dare to sell gasoline by the gallon.
I come back to the voluntary, democratic conversion to metric that we on this side want to see. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will address these specific questions. Will the Government agree to a tandem system of measurement in both Imperial and metric labelling on all packaging and advertising? Will the Government finally agree that Canadians need and deserve a freedom of choice and information when purchasing goods? Is this too much to ask in a democracy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-COMPULSORY ASPECT OF LAW ON ADVERTISING. (B) REQUEST THAT MEASUREMENTS BE PERMITTED IN BOTH IMPERIAL AND METRIC SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the second night in a row I have the opportunity of addressing this problem. The Hon. Member does not like the word "dinosaur". Perhaps Neanderthal would suit him better.
I should first of all like to correct one misstatement made again by the Hon. Member opposite. The Minister at his press conference on December 13 pointed out that an error had been made in the Kasparian case in that charges against Mrs. Kasparian were made under the wrong section of the Act. It is unfortunate that this area has been capitalized on by Members of the Opposition in that they have implied that the Act itself is in question. This is not so. The Act is not at all in question. This is a matter, as I said, of charges being laid under the wrong section.
Furthermore, I wish to advise the Hon. Member that the present regulations regarding the use of metric units in the retail sale and advertising of home furnishings, gasoline and diesel fuel, and individually weighed food products, were adopted at the express request of the volunteer committees representing these three sectors of our economy.
It is true also that the vast majority of manufacturers and retailers in Canada wish to continue with the sole use of metric units in trade.
The Hon. Member addressed a specific question to me. He asked whether the Government would agree to a tandem system of labelling. I would say that the Member and his Party
December 21, 1982

are also concerned that consumers be able to verify price increases. To allow both systems, for example, in the area of retail scales would put the consumer into a much weaker position. If one week grapes or potatoes were sold in Imperial units and the following week they were sold in metric units, clearly a shopper would not be able to tell from week to week whether there had been an increase or a decrease in the price of those units.
I would suggest that if Hon. Members opposite were really interested in promoting the interests of the consumer, there are certain propositions they might make which could be deemed reasonable and could be discussed in a reasonable fashion. The manner in which most of them conduct themselves, by going on the kind of witch hunt they have been engaged in in recent months, certainly does not lead to a reasonable or satisfactory conclusion of this matter.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: INCOME TAX-REVIEW OF TAX ASSESSMENTS FOR YOUTH FOR CHRIST WORKERS. (B) ATTITUDE OF TAX OFFICIALS
INCOME TAX-REVIEW OF TAX ASSESSMENTS FOR YOUTH FOR CHRIST WORKERS. (B) ATTITUDE OF TAX OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to discuss a serious topic after having listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). We have heard the old adage now and again that if you have a weak argument, you should talk louder.
Last week, Mr. Speaker, I raised a question with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) that is very serious for me. I raised a very important issue in regard to the role of National Revenue and charitable organizations. I am concerned about the intention of the National Revenue Department to go after charitable organizations such as the one I mentioned last week, namely Youth for Christ. I might say at the outset that I was pleased with the way the Minister responded to me. It was very evident to me that he did not know what was happening out there. He was interested to make sure that justice was done.
I am pleased to say tonight that he has already responded to me by mail and has given me a partial answer to my question and a commitment that he will be working on it in the future to make sure that these people are not hard done by the Government. I am pleased to tell the House that that has happened.
I am also concerned about the principle involved. 1 say again that I am sure the Minister will deal fairly with these particular cases. One of the principles concerned is that the federal Government seems, in that case, to be making a major and costly effort to collect very minimal taxes from very low income people. It will cost the taxpayers in cost effectiveness much more than it is worth. I understand you cannot apply it universally. However, when it comes to low income groups, particularly this bracket, it seems to me to be counterproductive to go into a re-assessment policy in order to collect taxes that historically should not have been collected.
Second, these community workers in question are very effective in the community dealing with those young people who have either been in trouble with the law, in trouble at
Adjournment Debate
school or perhaps have become school drop-outs. At any rate, they are not facing a future of being productive and creative citizens in our country.
The workers who have been among these young people have been very effective in working with them. 1 suggest that these community workers who are being paid by voluntary gifts through charitable donations through the organization will be driven out of this work, if the cost of their work increases dramatically because of increased taxes, and they will move into something else where they can earn more to keep body and soul together. This will either leave that work vacant and undone or make the Government do the work.
It seems to me that it is usually better in these situations if people do the work on a voluntary basis rather than have a Government agency do the work. The net effect of vacating the field and leaving it to the Government would be detrimental to this kind of community work that is presently being done by voluntary agencies. The net effect of that would be an increased cost to the community. If we consider this in pure cost effective dollars, I believe that it is counterproductive to go after voluntary agencies like this to see how much more tax money we can extract from them.
The question I raised last week was another policy question; if the Department of National Revenue feels that it must reassess its policy with respect to these workers, why not begin by approaching the officers of the national organization? Why approach individual workers who are overloaded with work, underpaid and sometimes hard pressed to pay the attention necessary to fight this additional battle? Why should they be strung out further when National Revenue, if nothing else, could go in compassion to the national organization and discuss a policy with it so that youth workers could concentrate on youth work rather than on defending themselves from the National Revenue officers.
The question that I would like to leave is an over-all question that 1 mentioned last week, and that is the matter of courtesy of those faceless officers who work in the large centres and deal with the telephone requests that come to them. It seems to me that I have heard this complaint more than anything else from individual taxpayers, regardless of whether they were community workers or not.
When a taxpayer calls a National Revenue office he feels that he deserves a courteous response, and in some cases he gets anything but that. I would simply urge the Minister to reinforce all of those faceless-and I do not blame them for being faceless-workers manning the telephone banks in the National Revenue office to be sure that they feel the sense of pain, the sense of pressure that the taxpayer feels when he is calling them.
I want to end by thanking the Minister, and the Parliamentary Secretary who has been working with the Minister on this, for taking a personal interest in this matter and getting us on the road to solving this, so that these community workers can

December 21, 1982
Adjournment Debate
do the work they have been called to do and want to do, rather than defend themselves from the Government.

subtopic: TRADE-STATUS OF NEGOTIATIONS ON EUROPEAN AIRBUS PROJECT. (B) REASONS FOR SELECTION OF AIRBUS PROJECT
TRADE-STATUS OF NEGOTIATIONS ON EUROPEAN AIRBUS PROJECT. (B) REASONS FOR SELECTION OF AIRBUS PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I want to discuss the Government's proposal to build a $500 million plant in Quebec to manufacture parts for the controversial A-320 for Airbus Industries of France.
It is one thing to bail out domestic companies such as Massey-Ferguson and Chrysler, which are well established firms and whose loss could greatly damage our economy, but it is another thing to dish out hundreds of millions of sorely needed dollars to a foreign consortium manufacturing a product for which I intend to show the market is mediocre at best, at the expense of aircraft manufacturers operating here.
I have already brought up the matter in the House and I have received what I feel is an evasive reply. I get the feeling that the whole Airbus affair has been shrouded in a veil of secrecy, which to me is totally unacceptable.
When I asked a question in the House on this matter of the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Regan), who ought to be up to date on such issues as this, it did not please me to have the buck passed to another Minister. On many occasions I have stood here to comment on the increasing lack of accountability and the diminishing respect for the Members of this House of Commons. We have heard little mention of this project in the House of Commons and we want clear, forthright answers as to the status of the dealings with Airbus Industries and some convincing statistics to show that this is really beneficial for all concerned.
In The Citizen this morning I read of another project which, if not nipped in the bud, could join Airbus Industrie as the next example of wool being pulled over the eyes of the Canadian public. It involves radar systems for modernization of airports across Canada, and shows just how cosy the Canadian and French Governments are getting.
Five companies bid for the contract of a new and modern system of radar in 30 airports across this country. An interdepartmental committee reported to Cabinet its recommendations for the two finalists in the competition. An obscure French company called Thomson was not one of the finalists. However, upon the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) return to Canada from France this fall, he ordered a review of the choice of finalists. So do not be surprised if, in a few years, one comes flying into Toronto on an A-320 which is guided into the airport on a Thomson radar system.
As the Member of Parliament for Erie, where a major manufacturer of aircraft components is located, I must ask the
Government what the effect of locating a new aircraft factory in Canada will be. Who will its suppliers be? Furthermore, if Airbus grabs a portion of the market from Boeing and McDonnell Douglas aircraft, plants such as Fleet Industries will almost certainly suffer.
The plant in Fort Erie, in my riding, employs upward of
1,000	people. Loss of business for this operation means unemployment and layoffs in many related sectors. In other large manufacturing centres, such as Malton, the results of competition with the A-320 could indeed be catastrophic.
The decision to subsidize Airbus is an unwise one in the light of current economic realities in the air transport industry. Flights are being cut back due to the high cost of fuel and the lack of demand. Is this a good time to introduce a new airplane? Consider the new aircraft just put out by boeing, the 767. Here is a fuel efficient aircraft which is effective in the medium range market, for which the A-320 is also designed. McDonnell Douglas will be offering similar designs in the very near future.
If one considers the volume of business that these companies do with Canada, it would be wise to stop and think about taking measures which would reduce this cash inflow. Boeing alone bought $147 million worth of Canadian aircraft components in the year 1981. Thus, we have the case of an aircraft which will be competing with at least five other models, the redesigned DC-9, the 757, the 767, the 737 from Boeing, and the latest entry from McDonnell Douglas which will be the D-3300. Therefore, there is a possibility that the A-320 will not even make it in the marketplace, and if it does not, that is another $500 million down the drain. If it succeeds and takes the profit away from the competition, we will lose anyway because of increased unemployment and lost business in the parts manufacturing plants.
The latest blow to independent entrepreneurs is the appearance of Airbus which will be, in effect, a Government subsidized product, competing against private companies. Airbus has been nurtured to the tune of $5 billion by European Governments. Thus, it will not have to bear a price tag necessitated by manufacturing costs. Its prices can be as low as it wishes. Thus, other manufacturers will have to lower their prices to compete. Any profit which Canadian companies are making now will be nullified by this giant company, and we will all feel the effects in increased costs and poor growth in the industry.
Before jumping into the deal with Airbus, 1 hope that the Government will consider the possible effects of its decision. Both McDonnell Douglas and Boeing may decide to cut back on production if they feel that the Government support to Airbus would result in a favoured position for Airbus products. In other words, Air Canada, a Crown corporation, might be pressured by the Government to buy Airbus products. The resultant unemployment could more than offset the newly created jobs in Quebec by Airbus.
December 21, 1982

In conclusion, it is my hope that the Ministers responsible will assess the facts in an unbiased and nonpartisan way so that the decision made reflects the wishes of the Canadian people and will benefit the workers and taxpayers of this nation.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRADE-STATUS OF NEGOTIATIONS ON EUROPEAN AIRBUS PROJECT. (B) REASONS FOR SELECTION OF AIRBUS PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to point out to my hon. friend opposite that the Canadian Government will indeed take into consideration all the concerns he expressed earlier, namely that we make sure there will be a good market for this operation, that the work will still be done here in this country, and that it will be a successful financial and industrial endeavour.
I would point out now that recently there has been a meeting with the de Havilland and Airbus Industries. The talks were very warm and generally speaking relatively good progress has been made; furthermore both parties so far seem to be satisfied with the negotiations. Of course, in such dealings, a lot of things have to be taken into consideration and as was pointed out earlier by the Hon. Member, a number of airlines now experiencing financial difficulties have decided to wait another year before officially introducing the Airbus, which means that in fact negotiations may progress somewhat more slowly than originally expected.
Another point that perhaps should be emphasized, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that very soon there will be other meetings between Airbus and de Havilland on the commercial aspect of the operation and the industrial aspect as well for the actual manufacturing of certain components of the Airbus 320 Aircraft, following which the Minister of course will be in a
Adjournment Debate
position to report to the House on the exact status of the negotiations.
I would also like to point out at this stage that we have no intention of casting aside the North American partner as far as aircraft manufacturing is concerned. Not at all. It is simply a matter for the Canadian Government to expand its market and developing its technology with a view to allowing our young and not so young workers to work in a field of high technology on what clearly is state-of-the-art jobs, both at the computer and avionics levels, what I would like to stress is that once more we shall continue manufacturing in Canada various components for the DC-9, such as the fuselage and wings, and ensuring that with both Boeing and McDonnell Douglas we will still contribute to industrial exchanges in an effort to promote avionics on the North American aircraft models.
But this does not preclude finding other markets in Europe and other continents provided it remains consistent with the spirit outlined earlier by the Hon. Member, namely to first ensure that we will safeguard the existing market and second that jobs will be going to the workers of this nation before those in other countries.
Therefore I would like to reassure the Hon. Member at this point. All his concerns are being taken into consideration and when the study of the matter is more advanced, the department and the Minister will be pleased to brief the House for the benefit of interested Members.
